content.text: Everything around us is made of tiny particles (atoms and molecules) that are constantly moving. The kinetic particle model (also called the kinetic theory) explains how the behaviour of these particles determines the properties of matter we can see and measure.

The kinetic particle model explains macroscopic properties of matter (such as pressure, volume, and state) by describing the microscopic behaviour of particles -- their arrangement, movement, and the forces between them.
All matter is made of particles
The smallest unit of an element (e.g., a gold atom)
Two or more atoms bonded together (e.g., H₂O, O₂)
Atoms or molecules with electric charge

Solid: Regular, closely packed
  +---+---+---+---+
  | o | o | o | o |
  +---+---+---+---+
  | o | o | o | o |
  +---+---+---+---+
  | o | o | o | o |
  +---+---+---+---+
  (particles vibrate in fixed positions)
Strong forces of attraction between particles

Liquid: Close but irregularly arranged
    o  o   o  o
   o  o  o   o
    o   o  o  o
   o  o   o   o
  (particles slide past each other)
but not in a regular pattern
Weaker forces of attraction than solids
No fixed shape, but fixed volume

Gas: Widely spaced, random motion
  o -->          o
          o            <-- o
     o         o -->
               <-- o
  o                   o
  (particles move fast in random directions)
No fixed shape, no fixed volume
The average kinetic energy of particles is directly proportional to the absolute temperature:
Absolute scale starting at absolute zero
Absolute zero (0 K = -273°C): Particles have minimum energy
Temperature in kelvin = temperature in Celsius + 273. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (0 K = -273 degrees C), where particles have the minimum possible energy.
is the random, jerky movement of small visible particles (like pollen grains in water or smoke particles in air).

Brownian Motion: Random path of a pollen grain

  start

       \/       \
        \    /---/

  (jerky, unpredictable zigzag path)
Caused by collisions with invisible molecules
Provides evidence that molecules are in constant motion
is the spreading out of particles from high concentration to low concentration.
Faster at higher temperatures (particles move faster)
Example: Smell spreading across a room
Particles move faster and take up more space
Explains why gaps are left between railway tracks
Students often say that particles themselves expand when heated. In reality, the particles do not change size -- they simply move faster and the average distance between them increases.
Explain why the smell of perfume spreads across a room.

Perfume molecules leave the liquid and enter the air. These molecules move randomly in all directions, colliding with air molecules. Through diffusion, the perfume molecules spread from high concentration (near the source) to low concentration (across the room). This random motion eventually distributes the molecules throughout the room.
Describe what happens to the particles in ice as it is heated from -10°C to 110°C.
Particles vibrate faster as temperature increases
Energy breaks bonds between particles; arrangement becomes less ordered
Particles move around each other faster as temperature increases
Energy breaks more bonds; particles escape the liquid
Particles move very fast with large spaces between them
Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of a container:
More particles in the same volume = higher pressure
Heating provides energy to break bonds between particles
At melting/boiling points, energy goes into breaking bonds, not increasing temperature
— The particles themselves don't change size; they just move faster and spread further apart.
— The spaces in solids are essentially empty (vacuum), not filled with air.
— They don't move from place to place, but they do vibrate.
— Particles only stop at absolute zero (0 K), which is unattainable.
"Gas particles move in straight lines until they hit walls"
— They collide frequently with each other, not just walls.

All matter is made of particles that are constantly moving
Particles vibrate in fixed positions, closely packed
Particles move around each other, close together
Particles move randomly at high speed, far apart
Higher temperature = faster particles = more kinetic energy
Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature
Evidence includes Brownian motion and diffusion
The model explains pressure, expansion, and changes of state
Particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. Strong forces hold them in place. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Particles are close together but irregularly arranged. They can move around each other, giving water no fixed shape but a fixed volume. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds in all directions. Very weak forces act between them. (explanation with physics reasoning)

is the random, jerky movement of small visible particles (e.g. pollen grains in water). It is caused by collisions with invisible molecules moving at high speed. This provides evidence that molecules exist and are in constant random motion, supporting the kinetic particle model. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The ink spreads faster in hot water.
At higher temperatures, water molecules have greater kinetic energy and move faster. They collide with ink particles more frequently and with more force, causing faster diffusion. (comparison)
Gases have large spaces between particles

, so when pressure is applied the particles can be pushed closer together. In liquids, particles are already close together with minimal space, so there is almost no room for compression. (explanation with physics reasoning)
In liquids, particles can slide past each other
, so the liquid flows to match the container shape. In solids, strong forces hold particles in fixed positions, maintaining a rigid shape. (explanation with physics reasoning)
On a hot day the air temperature is higher

, so gas particles inside the tyre move faster. They collide with the tyre walls more frequently and with greater force, increasing the pressure and making the tyre feel harder. (explanation with physics reasoning)
